[[File:Боевой многофункциональный робототехнический комплекс Уран-9 - Международного военно-технического форума АРМИЯ-2016 01.jpg|thumb|[[Uran-9]] unmanned ground vehicle]]

An '''unmanned ground vehicle''' ('''UGV''') also known colloquially as '''armored robot''' ('''ARB'''{{Citation needed|date=August 2025}}) is a [[vehicle]] that operates while in contact with the ground without an onboard human presence. UGVs can be used for many applications where it is inconvenient, dangerous, expensive, or impossible to use an onboard human operator. Typically, the vehicle has [[sensors]] to observe the environment, and [[autonomous]]ly controls its behavior or uses a remote human operator to control the vehicle via [[teleoperation]].

The UGV is the land-based counterpart to [[unmanned aerial vehicle]]s, [[unmanned underwater vehicle]]s and [[unmanned surface vehicle]]s. Unmanned robots are used in war<ref>{{Cite news |title=Ukraine is inching towards robot-on-robot fighting |url=https://www.economist.com/europe/2025/06/26/ukraine-is-inching-towards-robot-on-robot-fighting |access-date=2025-08-03 |newspaper=The Economist |issn=0013-0613}}</ref> and by civilians.

{{Toclimit}}

==History==
[[File:Radio_Controlled_Car_1921.jpg|thumb|right|RCA radio controlled car. Dayton, Ohio, 1921]]

In 1904, Spanish engineer [[Leonardo Torres Quevedo]] was developing a radio-based control system, which he named ''Telekino''. He chose to conduct an initial test in the form of a three-wheeled land vehicle ([[tricycle]]), which had an effective range of 20 to 30 meters, the first known example of an unmanned ground vehicle.<ref>{{cite book |author=H. R. Everett |title=Unmanned Systems of World Wars I and II |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |date=2015 |pages=91–95 |isbn=978-0-262-02922-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Alfred |first=Randy |title= Remote Control Wows Public |url=https://www.wired.com/2011/11/1107wireless-remote-control/ |access-date=2024-05-01 |magazine=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028}}</ref>

The first prototypes of explosive robotic drones were Aubriot-Gabet 'land torpedoes' invented in [[France]] in 1915<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://modelarchives.free.fr/Bestiaire/Torpter_P/|title=Modelstories|website=modelarchives.free.fr}}</ref> and the Crocodile [[Schneider-Creusot]]. Twenty examples were put into service with the [[2nd Army (France)|2nd French Army]] in July 1915.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://forum.pages14-18.com/viewtopic.php?t=53464|title=Crocodile Schneider - Forum PAGES 14-18|website=forum.pages14-18.com}}</ref>

A working remote-controlled car was reported in the October 1921 issue of [[RCA Corporation|RCA]]'s ''World Wide Wireless'' magazine. The car was controlled wirelessly via radio; it was thought the technology could be adapted to tanks.<ref>{{cite journal |title= Radio Controlled Cars |journal= World Wide Wireless |date= October 1921 |volume= 2 |url= https://archive.org/stream/WorldWideWirelessV2#page/n341/mode/2up |page= 18 |access-date= May 20, 2016}}</ref> In the 1930s, the [[USSR]] developed the [[Teletank]], a small tank, armed with a machine gun. It was remotely controlled by radio from another tank. Teletanks operated in the [[Winter War]] (1939–1940) between Finland and the USSR and at the start of the [[Eastern Front (World War II)|German-Soviet War]] after Germany [[Operation Barbarossa|invaded the USSR]] in 1941. During World War II, the British developed a radio-controlled version of their [[Matilda II]] infantry tank in 1941. Known as "Black Prince", it would have been used for drawing the fire of concealed anti-tank guns, or for demolition missions. Due to the costs of converting the transmission system of the tank to [[Preselector gearbox#Wilson gearbox|Wilson-type gearboxes]], an order for 60 tanks was cancelled.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fletcher |first=David |url={{google books|plainurl=y|id=8_FUvgAACAAJ|page=40}} |title=Matilda Infantry Tank 1938–45 |date=1994-01-27 |publisher=Bloomsbury USA |isbn=978-1-85532-457-2 |language=en|page=40}}</ref>

From 1942, the German {{lang | de | [[Wehrmacht]]}} used the [[Goliath tracked mine]] for remote-controlled demolition work. The Goliath was a tracked vehicle carrying 60 kg of explosive charge, directed through a control cable. It modeled a miniature French tracked vehicle found after the [[Battle of France|German defeat of France]] in 1940. The combination of cost, low speed, reliance on a cable for control, and poor protection against weapons, meant that the Goliath was not considered a success.

The first major mobile robot development effort, named [[Shakey the robot|"Shakey"]], took place during the 1960s as a research study for the U.S. [[DARPA|Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency]] (DARPA). Shakey was a wheeled platform that had a TV camera, sensors, and a computer to help guide its tasks of picking up wooden blocks and placing them in certain areas based on commands. DARPA subsequently developed a series of autonomous and semi-autonomous ground robots, often in conjunction with the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]]. As part of the [[Strategic Computing Initiative]] of 1983–1993, DARPA {{circa | 1985}} demonstrated the Autonomous Land Vehicle,<ref>

UGVs rose in significance after the full-scale [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]] and the dramatic rise in use of unmanned aerial vehicles. On March 29, 2024, as part of the [[Eastern Ukraine campaign|Eastern Ukraine Campaign]], a platoon of Russian UGVs equipped with [[AGS-17]] automatic grenade launchers was deployed for an assault near the town of [[Berdychi]] in Ukraine, marking the first ever use of UGVs for direct frontline assaults.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://militarnyi.com/en/news/russian-forces-deploy-ugvs-armed-with-ags-17-grenade-launchers/|title=Russian Forces Deploy UGVs Armed with AGS-17 Grenade Launchers |date=March 29, 2024 |first=Vadim |last=Kushnikov |work=Militarnyi}}</ref>{{unreliable source?|date=March 2025}}

During an undated operation, the 3rd Assault Brigade claimed the world's first surrender of enemy soldiers to unmanned drones in the Kharkiv Oblast. FPV and ground drones were used to attack the Russian positions. As more ground drones approached the position, the Russians opted to surrender. The Ukrainian ground drones then guided the Russians soldiers to the Ukrainian position where they surrendered. The press release read: "For the first time in history: Russian soldiers surrendered to the 3rd Assault Brigade's ground drones,".<ref>{{Cite news |author=Anna Fratsyvir |date=2025-07-09 |title= In historic feat, Ukraine's 3rd Brigade captures Russian troops using only drones and robots, military says |url= https://kyivindependent.com/ukrainian-assault-brigade-captures-russian-troops-using-only-drones-and-robots-in-historic-operation-military-says-06-2025/ |access-date=2025-07-09 |work=The Kyiv Independent}}</ref>

On 22 December 2025, the [[3rd Assault Brigade]] said that a Ukrainian UGV, a Droid TW 12.7 armed with a .50-caliber machine gun, held off Russian attacks for 45 days while being operated either remotely or using AI. The first time a position was held solely by an UGV without direct human support such as infantry.<ref>{{Cite web |author= Matthew Loh |date=2025-12-23 |title= Ukrainian troops say a 'droid' with a .50-cal machine gun held off Russian attacks for 45 days in a row |url= https://www.businessinsider.com/ukrainians-devdroid-tw-50-cal-gun-russians-days-2025-12 |access-date=2025-12-25|website=Business Insider|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Design==
UGVs generally include: a [[Weapons platform|vehicle platform]], [[sensor]]s, [[control system]]s, guidance interface, communication links, and [[System integration|systems integration]] features.<ref name="GRRC">{{cite web|last1=Nguyen-Huu|first1=Phuoc-Nguyen|last2=Titus|first2=Joshua|title=GRRC Technical Report 2009-01 Reliability and Failure in Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV)|url=http://arc.engin.umich.edu/grrc/techreports/200901_ReliabilityUGV.pdf|publisher=University of Michigan|access-date=3 September 2016|archive-date=27 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160527114009/http://arc.engin.umich.edu/grrc/techreports/200901_ReliabilityUGV.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Platform===
The platform can be a car, truck, [[all-terrain vehicle]], etc., and includes the locomotive apparatus, sensors, and power source. Tracks, wheels, and legs are common forms of locomotion. The platform may include an articulated body and may join with other units.<ref name="GRRC" /><ref name="Gerhart">{{cite book|last1=Gerhart|first1=Grant|last2=Shoemaker|first2=Chuck|title=Unmanned Ground Vehicle Technology|date=2001|publisher=SPIE-International Society for Optical Engine|isbn=978-0819440594|page=97|url={{google books|plainurl=y|id=x99SAAAAMAAJ}}|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref> Power sources can be [[internal combustion engine]]s, batteries, or hydrogen.<ref>{{Cite journal|url = https://www.unidir.org/publication/uncrewed-ground-systems-primer|title = Uncrewed Ground Systems: A Primer|date = 19 October 2022|website = United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research|last1=Grand-Clément |first1=Sarah |last2=Bajon|first2=Theò}}</ref>

===Sensors===
Sensors create a model of the environment, showing other vehicles, pedestrians, and obstacles. They also locate the vehicle on the navigation path. Sensors can include compasses, odometers, inclinometers, gyroscopes, cameras, laser and ultrasound rangefinders, GPS radios, and infrared technology.<ref name="GRRC" /><ref name="Sensors">{{citation|last=Demetriou|first=Georgios|title=A Survey of Sensors for Localization of Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs)|publisher=[[Frederick Institute of Technology]]|citeseerx=10.1.1.511.710}}</ref>

===Control systems===
Unmanned ground vehicles are generally considered [[Remote operated vehicle|Remote-Operated]] or [[Autonomous]], although [[Supervisory control|Supervisory Control]] is a combination of autonomous and remote operation.<ref name="Gage">{{cite journal|last1=Gage|first1=Douglas|title=UGV HISTORY 101: A Brief History of Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) Development Efforts|journal=Unmanned Systems Magazine|date=Summer 1995|volume=13|issue=3|url=http://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a422845.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303171624/http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a422845.pdf|url-status=live|archive-date=March 3, 2016|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref>

[[File:Guardium001.jpg|thumb|right|[[Guardium]] used by the [[Israel Defense Forces]] to operate as part of the border security operations]]

====Autonomous====
[[File:ARV-A-L.jpg|right|thumb|A US Army [[XM1219 armed robotic vehicle]]. Canceled in 2011.]]

An autonomous UGV (AGV) is an [[autonomous robot]] that replaces the human controller with [[artificial intelligence]] technologies. The vehicle uses sensors to feed a model of the environment, which supports a control system that determines the next action. This eliminates the need for humans to watch over the vehicle.

An autonomous vehicle must have the ability to:
* Navigate based on maps that allow the vehicle to pick a route from origin to destination.
* Detect objects such as people and vehicles.
* Travel between [[waypoint]]s without human assistance.
* Avoid harming people, property or itself, unless those are part of its mission.

A robot may also be able to learn autonomously. Autonomous learning includes the ability to:
* Gain capabilities.
* Adjust strategies based on the surroundings.
* Adapt to surroundings.
* Behave ethically in pursuit of mission goals.

Armed autonomous machines must distinguish between combatants and civilians. This is particularly true in conflicts where combatants intentionally disguise themselves as civilians to avoid detection. Even highly accurate but imperfect systems can pose unacceptable civilian losses.

===Guidance interface===
The interface between the machine and the human operator can include a [[joystick]], autonomous software, or voice commands.<ref name="GRRC" />

===Communication links===
Communication between UGV and control station can be done via radio or [[fiber optics]]. It may include communication with other machines and robots.<ref name="GRRC" />

===Systems integration===
The various hardware and software elements must work together to produce desired results.<ref name="GRRC" /><ref name="Ge">{{cite book|last1=Ge|first1=Shuzhi Sam|title=Autonomous Mobile Robots: Sensing, Control, Decision Making and Applications|date=4 May 2006|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781420019445|page=584|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3WvLBQAAQBAJ|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref>

==Uses==
A wide variety of UGVs were in use as of 2025. They typically replace humans in hazardous situations, such as handling [[explosive]]s and in [[Bomb disposal#Techniques|bomb disabling vehicles]], where additional strength or smaller size is needed, or where humans cannot safely go. Military applications include surveillance, reconnaissance, and target acquisition.<ref name="Gage" /> They are used in industries such as agriculture, mining, and construction.<ref name="Hebert">{{cite book|last1=Hebert|first1=Martial|last2=Thorpe|first2=Charles|last3=Stentz|first3=Anthony|title=Volume 388 of the series The Springer International Series in Engineering and Computer Science|date=2007|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4613-7904-1|pages=1–17|chapter=Intelligent Unmanned Ground Vehicles|doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-6325-9_1}}</ref> UGVs are effective in naval operations, and for the [[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] in combat; they can help in logistics operations on land and sea.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/11379/autonomous-vehicles-in-support-of-naval-operations|title=Autonomous Vehicles in Support of Naval Operations|last=Committee on Autonomous Vehicles in Support of Naval Operations|first=National Research Council|date=2005|publisher=National Academies Press|doi=10.17226/11379|bibcode=2005nap..book11379N |isbn=978-0-309-09676-8}}</ref>

UGVs are under development for [[peacekeeping]] operations, ground surveillance, gatekeeper/checkpoint operations, urban street presence and to enhance police and military raids in urban settings. UGVs can "draw first fire" from adversaries—reducing military and police casualties.<ref>{{cite web|title=Cry Havoc and Let Slip the Bots of War|url=https://www.glenair.com/qwikconnect/pdf/2013-july.pdf|website=QwikConnect|publisher=Glenair|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref> Furthermore, UGVs are used in rescue and recovery mission and were used to find survivors following [[9/11]] at [[World Trade Center site|Ground Zero]].<ref name="Disaster Response">{{cite web|title=Drones for Disaster Response and Relief Operations|url=http://www.issuelab.org/resources/21683/21683.pdf|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref> In Hong Kong, the police and other workers use driverless vehicles.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.passengerselfservice.com/2022/03/hong-kong-airport-now-has-4-unmanned-patrol-cars/|title=Hong Kong Airport's unmanned patrol cars|date=March 16, 2022}}</ref>

===Space ===
{{Main|Rover (space exploration)}}
{{Globalize|section|USA|date=March 2025}}
[[NASA]]'s [[Mars Exploration Rover]] project included two UGVs, Spirit and Opportunity. Both performed beyond design parameters. This is attributed to redundant systems, careful handling, and long-term interface decision-making.<ref name="GRRC" /> [[Opportunity (rover)|Opportunity]] and its twin, [[Spirit (rover)|Spirit]], are six-wheeled, solar-powered ground vehicles. They were launched in July 2003 and landed on opposite sides of [[Mars]] in January 2004. Spirit operated nominally until it became trapped in deep sand in April 2009, lasting more than 20 times longer than expected.<ref name="Space">{{cite web|last1=Wolchover|first1=Natalie|title=NASA Gives Up On Stuck Mars Rover Spirit|url=http://www.space.com/11773-nasa-mars-rover-spirit-mission-ends.html|website=Space.com|date=24 May 2011 |access-date=12 September 2016}}</ref> Opportunity was operational for more than 14 years beyond its intended lifespan of three months. [[Curiosity (rover)|Curiosity]] landed on Mars on 6 August 2012, and its original two-year mission has since been extended until October 2025 ({{age in days|6 August 2012|1 October 2025}} days longer than expected).<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA Planetary Mission Senior Reviews - PMSR - NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/planetary-science/resources/senior-review/ |access-date=2025-01-07 |website=science.nasa.gov |date=14 April 2022 |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Civilian and commercial ===
Civilian applications are automating processes in manufacturing environments.<ref name="Khosiawan">{{cite journal|last1=Khosiawan|first1=Yohanes|last2=Nielsen|first2=Izabela|title=A system of UAV application in indoor environment|journal=Production & Manufacturing Research|date=2016|volume=4|issue=1|pages=2–22|doi=10.1080/21693277.2016.1195304|doi-access=free}}</ref> They work as autonomous tour guides for the [[Carnegie Museum of Natural History]] and the Swiss National Exhibition Expo.<ref name="GRRC" />

====Agriculture====
[[File:Lemken, Agritechnica 2023, Hanover (P1160369).jpg|thumb|Autonomous tractor by [[Bernard Krone Holding|Krone]]]]

UGVs are one type of [[agricultural robot]]. Unmanned tractors can operate around the clock, to meet short windows for harvesting. UGVs are used for spraying and thinning.<ref name="Robot Report">{{cite web|last1=Tobe|first1=Frank|title=Are ag robots ready? 27 companies profiled|url=https://www.therobotreport.com/news/ag-in-transition-from-precision-ag-to-full-autonomy|website=The Robot Report|access-date=12 September 2016|date=2014-11-18}}</ref> They can be used to monitor crop and livestock health.<ref name="New Scientist">{{cite web|last1=Klein|first1=Alice|title=Cattle-herding robot Swagbot makes debut on Australian farms|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2097004-cattle-herding-robot-swagbot-makes-debut-on-australian-farms/|website=New Scientist|access-date=12 September 2016}}</ref>

====Manufacturing====
In the manufacturing environment, UGVs are used for transporting materials.<ref name="Borzemski">{{cite book|last1=Borzemski|first1=Leszek|last2=Grzech|first2=Adam|last3=Świątek|first3=Jerzy|last4=Wilimowska|first4=Zofia|title=Information Systems Architecture and Technology: Proceedings of 36th International Conference on Information Systems Architecture and Technology – ISAT 2015|date=2016|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319285559|page=31|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vGWhCwAAQBAJ|access-date=12 September 2016}}</ref> Aerospace companies use these vehicles for precision positioning and transporting heavy, bulky components between manufacturing stations, which is faster than using large cranes and can keep people out of dangerous areas.<ref name="Waurzyniak">{{cite journal|last1=Waurzyniak|first1=Patrick|title=Aerospace Automation Stretches Beyond Drilling and Filling|journal=Manufacturing Engineering|url=http://www.sme.org/aerospace-automation-stretches-beyond-drilling-and-filling/?taxid=3440|access-date=3 September 2016|archive-date=2 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220302235155/https://www.sme.org/aerospace-automation-stretches-beyond-drilling-and-filling/?taxid=3440|url-status=dead}}</ref>

====Mining====
UGVs can be used to traverse and map mine tunnels.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Hatfield|first1=Michael|title=Use of UAV and UGV for Emergency Response and Disaster Preparedness in Mining Applications|url=http://ine.uaf.edu/mirl/research/use-of-unmanned-aircraft-systems-uas-and-unmanned-ground-vehicles-ugv-for-emergency-response-and-disaster-preparedness-in-mining-applications/|access-date=3 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160916142743/http://ine.uaf.edu/mirl/research/use-of-unmanned-aircraft-systems-uas-and-unmanned-ground-vehicles-ugv-for-emergency-response-and-disaster-preparedness-in-mining-applications/|archive-date=16 September 2016|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref> Combining radar, laser, and visual sensors, UGVs are in development to map 3D rock surfaces in open pit mines.<ref name="Robotics Tomorrow">{{cite web|title=Robots Explore Dangerous Mines with Novel Fusion Sensor Technology|url=http://www.roboticstomorrow.com/article/2015/01/robots-explore-dangerous-mines-with-novel-sensor-fusion-technology/5403|website=Robotics Tomorrow|access-date=12 September 2016}}</ref>

====Supply chain====
In the warehouse management system, UGVs have multiple uses from transferring goods with autonomous forklifts and conveyors to stock scanning and taking inventory.<ref>{{cite web|title=Automation and Computers|url=http://automacomp.blogspot.com/2016/08/automation-in-warehouses.html?m=0|access-date=12 September 2016|date=2016-08-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=More robots, inside and outside the warehouse|url=http://www.tandlnews.com.au/2016/01/13/article/22927/|website=Transport and Logistics News|access-date=12 September 2016|archive-date=9 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009172802/http://www.tandlnews.com.au/2016/01/13/article/22927/|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Automated guided vehicle|Automated Guided Vehicles]] are extensively used in warehouses to deal with goods that are dangerous to humans (e.g. corrosive and flammable goods) or need special handling such as passing through freezers.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-01-18 |title=Smart Technologies for E-commerce Fulfillment {{!}} SIPMM Publications |url=https://publication.sipmm.edu.sg/smart-technologies-e-commerce-fulfillment/ |access-date=2022-07-13 |website=publication.sipmm.edu.sg |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Emergency response===
UGVs are used in many emergency situations including urban [[search and rescue]], firefighting, and nuclear response.<ref name="Disaster Response" /> Following the 2011 [[Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant]] accident, UGVs were used in Japan for mapping and structural assessment in areas with too much radiation to allow a human presence.<ref name="Siciliano">{{cite book|last1=Siciliano|first1=Bruno|last2=Khatib|first2=Oussama|title=Springer Handbook of Robotics|date=2016|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319325521|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RTvADAAAQBAJ&pg=PA1586|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref>

===Military ===

[[File:TEODor.jpg|thumbnail|right|"tEODor" robot of the [[German Army]] destroying a fake [[Improvised explosive device|IED]]]]

UGV use by the military has saved many lives. Applications include [[explosive ordnance disposal]] (EOD) such as landmines, loading heavy items, and repairing ground conditions under enemy fire.<ref name="Gage" /> The number of robots used in Iraq increased from 150 in 2004 to 5000 in 2005 where they disarmed over 1000 roadside bombs in Iraq at the end of 2005.<ref name=caraf>{{cite book|last1=Carafano |first1= J. |last2=Gudgel |first2=A. |year=2007 |title=The Pentagon's robots: Arming the future: Backgrounder 2093|pages= 1–6|publisher=[[The Heritage Foundation]]}}</ref> By 2013, the U.S. Army had purchased 7,000 such machines and 750 had been destroyed.<ref name="Popular Science">{{cite magazine|last1=Main|first1=Douglas|title=ROBOTS TO THE RESCUE, WHEN DISASTER STRIKES AND DANGER LOOMS, THE HEROES THAT BURST ONTO THE SCENE TO SAVE THE DAY MIGHT NOT EVEN BE HUMAN.|magazine=Popular Science|date=8 April 2013|url=http://www.popsci.com/trp-sponsored-article-slideshow}}</ref> The U.S. military is building UGVs to act as armed robots outfitted with machine guns and grenade launchers that may replace soldiers in combat. Such uses potentially pose ethical concerns by removing humans from the [[OODA loop]].<ref name="Atherton">{{cite magazine|last1=Atherton|first1=Kelsey|title=ROBOTS MAY REPLACE ONE-FOURTH OF U.S. COMBAT SOLDIERS BY 2030, SAYS GENERAL|magazine=Popular Science|date=22 January 2014|url=http://www.popsci.com/article/technology/robots-may-replace-one-fourth-us-combat-soldiers-2030-says-general|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref><ref name="Riga">Māris Andžāns, Ugis Romanovs. Digital Infantry Battlefield Solution. Concept of Operations. Part Two. –  Riga Stradins University.  – 2017. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/318792490_Digital_Infantry_Battlefield_Solution_Concept_of_Operations_Part_Two]</ref><ref name= Nerekhta/>

Another widespread application of UGVs gaining popularity is for [[Casualty evacuation|CASEVAC]]. During the full-scale [[Russo-Ukrainian War]], some Ukrainian units such as the [[13th Khartiia Brigade]], [[118th Mechanized Brigade (Ukraine)|118th Mechanized Brigade]], and 1st Separate Medical Battalion have started effectively using UGVs to evacuate wounded soldiers from the gray zone - sometimes under drone or artillery fire - for long distances of up to {{Convert|34|km|mi}}.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cherevko |first=Vlad |date=2025-08-09 |title=Zmii-500 ground drone of Khartiia Brigade rescues wounded soldier, covering distance of 34 km – video |url=https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2025/08/09/7525400/ |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=Ukrainska Pravda |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gubina |first=Evgenia |date=2025-08-08 |title=The 118th Mechanized Brigade showed how a ground robot was used to rescue a wounded soldier |url=https://oboronka.mezha.ua/en/nazemniy-robot-poryatunok-poranenogo-biycya-303892/ |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=Межа |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-21 |title="They set it on fire, but it kept going": MAUL withstood two FPV fits and a Massive Artillery Barrage |url=https://armyinform.com.ua/en/2025/12/21/they-set-it-on-fire-but-it-kept-going-maul-withstood-two-fpv-fits-and-a-massive-artillery-barrage/ |access-date=2025-12-23 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://music.youtube.com/watch?v=5Eet8g_B3J0|title=YouTube Music|website=YouTube Music}}</ref>

===Examples===
{{Update|part=section|date=May 2024|reason=Years-old info. This is a fast-moving field.}}

====SARGE====
SARGE is a 4-wheel drive all-terrain vehicle that uses the frame of the Yamaha Breeze. The objective is to provide each infantry battalion with up to eight SARGE units.<ref name=Singer2009b>{{Cite book |last=Singer |first=P. W. |url={{google books|plainurl=y|id=6aStP3Du5cgC}}|title=Wired for War: The Robotics Revolution and Conflict in the 21st Century |date=2009-01-22 |publisher=Penguin |isbn=978-1-4406-8597-2 |language=en}}</ref> SARGE is primarily used for remote surveillance; sent ahead of the infantry to investigate potential ambushes.

====Multi-Utility Tactical Transport====
Built by [[General Dynamics Land Systems]], the Multi-Utility Tactical Transport ("MUTT") comes in 4-, 6- and 8-wheeled variants. It was tested by the US Marine Corps in July 2016 and was selected for the US Army's Squad Multipurpose Equipment Transport (SMET) unmanned ground system requirement in November 2019. GDLS signed a $162.4m contract to deliver 624 UGVs through October 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Multi-Utility Tactical Transport (MUTT) UGV, United States of America |url=https://www.army-technology.com/projects/multi-utility-tactical-transport-mutt-ugv/ |access-date=2025-05-21 |website=Army Technology |language=en-US}}</ref>

====X-2====
X-2 is a medium-sized tracked UGV built by Digital Concepts Engineering. It is based on a previous autonomous robotic system designed for use in EOD, search and rescue (SAR), perimeter patrol, communications relay, mine detection and clearing, and as a light weapons platform. It measures 1.31 m in length, weighs 300 kg and can reach speeds of 5 km/h. It traverses slopes up to 45' steep and crosses deep mud. The vehicle is controlled using the Marionette system which is also used on [[Wheelbarrow (robot)|Wheelbarrow EOD robots]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Rovery|first1=Melanie|title=DSEI 2017: X-2 UGV emerges from agricultural role|url=http://www.janes.com/article/74111/dsei-2017-x-2-ugv-emerges-from-agricultural-role|website=janes.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=New X-2 Unmanned CBRN Detection Platform launched at DSEI 2017|url=https://www.armyrecognition.com/dsei_2017_news_online_show_daily_coverage_report_u/new_x-2_unmanned_cbrn_detection_platform_launched_at_dsei_2017.html|website=armyrecognition.com|date=12 September 2017 |access-date=7 December 2017}}</ref>

====The Warrior====
The Warrior is a new model of the [[PackBot]], but over five times its size. It can travel at speeds of up to 15 mph, and is the first PackBot capable of carrying a weapon.<ref name=Singer2009a>{{cite journal|last=Singer |first=P. |year=2009 |title=Military robots and the laws of war |journal=The New Atlantis: A Journal of Technology and Society |pages=23, 25–45}}</ref> Like the Packbot, it plays a key role in checking for explosives. They are capable of carrying 68 kilograms and travelling at 8 mph.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2007-06-26 |title=iRobot receives additional $1.6 million in TSWG funding to develop, train, test iRobot Warrior |url=https://doi.org/10.1108/ir.2007.04934dab.006 |journal=Industrial Robot|volume=34 |issue=4 |doi=10.1108/ir.2007.04934dab.006 |issn=0143-991X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

====TerraMax====
{{main|TerraMax (vehicle)}}

TerraMax is designed to be integrated into any tactical wheeled vehicle and is fully incorporated into the brakes, steering, engine, and transmission. Fitted vehicles retain the ability to be driver-operated. Vehicles manufactured by [[Oshkosh Corporation|Oshkosh Defense]] and fitted with the package competed in the DARPA Grand Challenges of 2004 and 2005, and the DARPA Urban Challenge of 2007. The Marine Corps Warfighting Lab selected TerraMax-equipped [[Medium Tactical Vehicle Replacement|MTVR]]s for the Cargo UGV project initiated in 2010, culminating in a technology concept demonstration for the Office of Naval Research in 2015. Demonstrated uses for the upgraded vehicles include unmanned route clearance (with a mine roller) and reducing personnel required for transportation convoys.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

====THeMIS====
{{main|THeMIS}}

THeMIS (Tracked Hybrid Modular Infantry System) is a ground-based armed drone vehicle designed largely for military applications. It is built by [[Milrem Robotics]] in Estonia. The vehicle's open architecture gives it multi-mission capability. Its main purpose is to increase situational awareness, provide improved intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance over wide areas, support on-base logistics, provide last-mile resupply for frontline units, and aid [[battle damage assessment]]. The vehicle serves as a transport platform, remote weapon station, [[IEDs|IED]] detection and disposal unit, etc. It reduces physical and cognitive load, increases standoff distance, force protection, and survivability.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

THeMIS Combat UGV includes an integrated self-stabilizing remote-controlled weapon system that provides direct fire support for manoeuvre forces. The weapons system provides high precision over wide areas, day and night, increasing standoff distance, force protection, and survivability. They can be equipped with light or heavy machine guns, 40 mm grenade launchers, 30 mm autocannons, and Anti-Tank Missile Systems.

THeMIS ISR UGVs have multi-sensor intelligence gathering capabilities. The system can aid dismounted infantry units, border guard, and law enforcement agencies to collect and process raw information and decrease the reaction time for commanders.

====Type-X====
{{main|Type-X (unmanned ground vehicle)}}

The Type-X is a 12-tonne tracked and armored robotic combat vehicle designed and produced by [[Milrem Robotics]] in Estonia. Measuring 600 cm long, 290 cm wide, and 220 cm tall, this heavy-duty vehicle weighs in at 12,000 kg and can carry a maximum payload of 4,100 kg.<ref>{{Cite web |last=office_zzam |date=2023-04-02 |title=First UK trial of heavy Unmanned Ground Vehicles showcases innovative |url=https://armyrecognition.com/news/army-news/2023/first-uk-trial-of-heavy-unmanned-ground-vehicles-showcases-innovative-military-technology |access-date=2024-05-31 |website=armyrecognition.com |language=en-gb}}</ref> It can be fitted with either autocannon turrets up to 50 mm or various other weapons systems, such as ATGMs, SAMs, radars, mortars, etc.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

====Talon====
The Talon is primarily used for bomb disposal, and is waterproof at 100 ft depth so that it can search for explosives underwater. The Talon was first used in 2000, and over 3,000 units have been distributed worldwide. By 2004, The Talon had been used in over 20,000 separate missions. These missions largely consisted of situations that were considered to be too dangerous for humans.<ref name=caraf/> These can include entering booby-trapped caves, searching for [[IEDs]], or scouting a combat zone. The Talon can keep pace with a running soldier. It can operate for 7 days off of one battery charge and is capable of climbing stairs. It was used at Ground Zero during the recovery mission. Talon's durability is attested by one unit that fell off a bridge into a river; the operators turned the control unit back on and drove it out of the river.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

====SWORDS====
{{main|Foster-Miller TALON}}

SWORDS is a Talon robot with an attached weapon system. Shortly after the release of the Warrior, the SWORDS robot was designed and deployed. SWORDS is capable of mounting any weapon system weighing less than 300 pounds.<ref name="Singer2009a"/> In a matter of seconds, the user can fit weapons such as a grenade launcher, rocket launcher, or 50 caliber machine gun. SWORDS fire with high precision, hitting the bullseye of a target 70/70 times in one test.<ref name=Singer2009b/> They are capable of withstanding damage such as multiple 50 caliber rounds, or a fall from a helicopter onto concrete.<ref name="Singer2009b"/> In addition, the SWORDS robot is capable of making its way through difficult terrain, including underwater.<ref name="Singer2009a"/> In 2004, only four SWORDS units were in existence. It was named as one of the world's most amazing inventions by ''[[Time Magazine]]'' in 2004. The US Army deployed three to Iraq in 2007 but then cancelled support of the project.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

====Small Unit Mobility Enhancement Technology (SUMET)====
The SUMET system is a platform and hardware independent, low-cost electro-optical perception, localization, and autonomy package developed to convert a traditional vehicle into a UGV. It performs various autonomous maneuvers in austere/harsh off-road environments, without dependence on a human operator or on [[GPS]]. The SUMET system has been deployed on various tactical and commercial platforms and is open, modular, scalable and extensible.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 8, 2017 |title=Automated Driving Systems & UGVs |url=https://www.swri.org/industry/sensing-perception-automotive-software-unmanned-systems-automotive-software-electronics |website=Southwest Research Institute}}</ref>

====Autonomous Small Scale Construction Machine (ASSCM)====
The ASSCM is a civilian unmanned ground vehicle developed in [[Van Yüzüncü Yıl University|Yuzuncu Yil University]] via a grant from TUBITAK (Project code 110M396).<ref>{{cite web| url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/76313 | title=Kürüme i̇çi̇n küçük ölçekli̇ otonom i̇ş maki̇nesi̇ tasarimi ve üreti̇mi̇ (Design and production of small-scale autonomous work machines for plowing) | access-date=2024-01-26}}</ref> The vehicle is a low-cost small scale construction machine that can grade soft soil. The machine is capable of autonomous grading within a polygon once the polygon border is defined. The machine determines its position by CP-DGPS and direction by consecutive position measurements.

====Taifun-M====
In April 2014, the [[Russian Army]] unveiled Taifun-M UGV as a remote sentry to guard [[RS-24 Yars]] and [[RT-2PM2 Topol-M]] missile sites. The Taifun-M features laser targeting and a cannon to carry out reconnaissance and patrol, detect and destroy stationary or moving targets, and provide fire support for security personnel. They are remotely operated.<ref>[http://en.ria.ru/military_news/20140422/189307020/Russia-Shows-Off-World-Leading-Security-Bots-for-Missile-Bases.html Russia Shows Off World-Leading Security Bots for Missile Bases] – En.Ria.ru, 22 April 2014</ref><ref>[http://www.armyrecognition.com/april_2014_global_defense_security_news_uk/russian_army_to_use_unmanned_ground_robot_taifun-m_to_protect_yars_and_topol-m_missile_sites_2304143.html Russian army to use unmanned ground robot Taifun-M to protect Yars and Topol-M missile sites] – Armyrecognition.com, 23 April 2014</ref>

====UKAP====
[[Turkey]]'s unmanned ground vehicle Weapon Platform (UKAP) was developed by defense contractors Katmerciler and [[ASELSAN]]. The vehicle is equipped with the 12.7 mm SARP remote-controlled, stabilized weapon systems.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thedefensepost.com/2018/02/22/turkey-armed-unmanned-ground-vehicles-afrin-syria/|title=Turkey says armed unmanned ground vehicles to be used in Afrin|date=2018-02-22|website=The Defense Post|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.defenseworld.net/news/22380/Turkey___s_New_Armed_Unmanned_Armed_Vehicle____UKAP____To_Be_Exported_To_Asian_Region#.XnexV4hKiUk|title=Turkey's New Armed Unmanned Armed Vehicle 'UKAP' To Be Exported To Asian Region|website=www.defenseworld.net|access-date=2020-03-22|archive-date=2020-01-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200127145509/https://www.defenseworld.net/news/22380/Turkey___s_New_Armed_Unmanned_Armed_Vehicle____UKAP____To_Be_Exported_To_Asian_Region#.XnexV4hKiUk|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.yenisafak.com/en/video-gallery/technology/turkeys-unmanned-ground-vehicle-ready-for-duty-2191004|title=Turkey's unmanned ground vehicle ready for duty|last=Şafak|first=Yeni|website=Yeni Şafak|language=tr-TR|access-date=2020-03-22}}</ref>

====Ripsaw====
The [[Ripsaw (vehicle)|Ripsaw]] is a developmental [[unmanned ground combat vehicle]] designed and built by [[Howe & Howe Technologies]] for evaluation by the United States Army.<ref name = teel>{{Cite web | author=Teel, Roger A. | title=Ripsaw demonstrates capabilities at APG | website=The United States Army Homepage | url=https://www.army.mil/article/42405/ripsaw-demonstrates-capabilities-at-apg/}}</ref>

==== Riderless bike ====
The coModule electric bicycle is remotely operated via smartphone, with users able to accelerate, turn and brake the bike by tilting their device. The bike can drive autonomously in a closed environment.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.comodule.com/blog/2015/cycling-towards-autonomy|title=Blog — COMODULE|website=www.comodule.com|access-date=Feb 4, 2023|archive-date=March 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304122212/http://www.comodule.com/blog/2015/cycling-towards-autonomy|url-status=dead}}</ref>

extract:
An unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) also known colloquially as armored robot (ARB) is a vehicle that operates while in contact with the ground without an onboard human presence. UGVs can be used for many applications where it is inconvenient, dangerous, expensive, or impossible to use an onboard human operator. Typically, the vehicle has sensors to observe the environment, and autonomously controls its behavior or uses a remote human operator to control the vehicle via teleoperation.
The UGV is the land-based counterpart to unmanned aerial vehicles, unmanned underwater vehicles and unmanned surface vehicles. Unmanned robots are used in war and by civilians.
